introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer FOUR questions in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing at least ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, graph paper and two outline maps of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown: (a) Briefly describe the drainage characteristics of the map area. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Drainage of the Bakaka map area (6 marks).** Describe the streams and rivers, their pattern, density, direction of flow and relation to relief. Quote grid references from the sheet.

- **Network and pattern.** The area is drained by many short streams and a few larger rivers. In the forested hills the streams branch like the veins of a leaf, with tributaries joining the main stream at acute angles: a **dendritic** pattern, controlled by a fairly uniform underlying rock. Around isolated hills some streams radiate outwards from the summit (a local **radial** pattern).
- **Density.** The network appears dense in the high, dissected hills of the Forest Reserve (many small streams in V-shaped valleys) and more open on the cleared lower land in the north, where fewer streams are shown (to be checked on the sheet).
- **Direction of flow.** Streams flow from the high ground (hills of about 500 to 600 m) down the slopes into narrow valleys; the main valley in the east and centre runs roughly north to south from the Ekomto and Ekomdion area towards Mangamba, so the general drainage is downhill towards the south, where the valley floor lies at about 300 m (spot heights of the order of 300 m near Ekomdion and Mangamba).
- **Valley form and channel.** In the hills the valleys are narrow and steep-sided, with fairly straight channels. Near Mangamba the valley widens into a flat floor and the river shows **meanders** and a wider flood plain, with the land partly cleared and settled.
- **Other features.** No lake is shown; the streams carry names (for example the Mahongue in the north-east; other names are printed along the main valley) and tracks cross them by fords or small bridges. Some streams are drawn with dashes, that is, they are intermittent.
- **Relationship with relief.** The main rivers follow the lowest ground and the lines of weakness between the hills, so the contours form V-shapes pointing uphill wherever a stream crosses them.

*Answer scheme (6 marks): pattern 2; density 1; direction of flow 1; valley and channel characteristics 1; relation to relief or named example with grid reference 1.*

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Using map evidence only, briefly state the difficulties posed by relief in the development of the area. (6 marks)

(ii) Propose strategies that can be adopted to overcome the problems identified in b) i) above. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(b)(i) Difficulties posed by relief (6 marks).** Each difficulty must be backed by map evidence (contour spacing, spot heights, grid references).

1. **Steep slopes and rugged hills.** Over most of the centre and south of the map the contours are close together and form many closed rings, with summits of about 500 to 600 m (for example the elongated hill just south of Ekang Loe with a 600 m contour, and the high ridge on the western margin around northing 519-520). Slopes are too steep for easy road building, farming or house building.
2. **Isolation of settlements.** Mangamba, Nyamsa, Ndiang Ekom and Ekomdion lie in a narrow valley between hills, linked to the rest of the area by one track that follows the stream; the northern settlements (Manengole, Nkong Niny, Ebone) are separated from them by the hills of the reserve. Movement of people and goods is slow and costly.
3. **High cost of infrastructure.** Roads must wind round the hills and cross many streams, so many bridges, cuttings and embankments are needed; there is only one main tarred road, in the north. Electricity and water lines are also costly to lay.
4. **Little flat land.** Flat land for settlement, farms and industry is limited to the northern lowland and the narrow valley floor around Mangamba; this restricts agriculture and the growth of villages.
5. **Erosion, landslides and flooding.** Steep, cleared slopes are exposed to soil erosion and mass movement; the valley floors are liable to flooding in the rainy season.
6. **Relief and reserve.** The hills are covered by the Forest Reserve, so little of the high ground is open for development.

*Any 3 to 4 well-supported difficulties (about 1.5 marks each).*

**(b)(ii) Strategies to overcome them (4 marks).**

- Build and upgrade roads along contours and valley floors with proper drainage, culverts and bridges, and link the valley villages to the main road in the north (all-weather earth or tarred road).
- Terrace the slopes, plough along the contours, plant trees and cover crops (agroforestry) to check erosion and landslides on cultivated slopes.
- Concentrate new settlements, schools and health centres on the gentle lower ground and valley floors, away from steep slopes and flood-prone areas.
- Use small-scale solutions for isolated villages: mini-hydro or solar power, boreholes and gravity-fed water supply, footbridges, mobile services.
- Reafforest and protect the upper slopes and stream sources (this supports the Forest Reserve).

*Any four well-explained strategies (1 mark each).*

questions.enonce_markdown: (c) Using evidence from the map, identify and state TWO reasons why the northern part of the map is ideal for the location of a hospital. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Reasons why the northern part is ideal for a hospital (4 marks: 2 marks per reason, one for the reason and one for the map evidence).**

1. **Accessibility.** The northern part is crossed by the main tarred road, which runs from the south-west (Quartier 8 and Manjo Etam) through the Manengole villages to Nkong Niny and Ebone, and other roads and tracks branch off it. Patients, ambulances, staff and medicines can reach a hospital there quickly from many villages, including in the rainy season.
2. **Large and concentrated population (demand).** Most of the built-up area is found in the north: the linear villages along the road (Manjo Etam, Manengole I, II and 3, Nkong Niny 1 and 2, Ebone 1 and 2) are close together, so a hospital there serves the largest number of people within a short distance (threshold population), while the southern part is almost empty forest.
3. **Suitable site.** The land is lower, with gentler slopes and wider contour spacing than in the hills, and it is cleared (cultivated land and scattered trees) and outside the Forest Reserve, so there is room to build and expand without felling forest. It is also away from the narrow valley floors that flood.
4. **Services.** Settlement along the main road makes it easier to supply water, electricity and telephone services, and schools and markets nearby mean that other services are already present.

*Award marks for any TWO reasons with map evidence.*

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) You have been consulted to determine the level of transport network development in the area:

(i) Draw a topological diagram of the road network. Use the following settlements as nodes: Quartier 8, Manjo Etam, Manengole I, Manengole II, Manengole 3, Nkong Niny 1, Nkong Niny 2, Ebone 1, Ebone 2, Ekang Loe and Ekomto. (6 marks)

(ii) Using the beta index, determine the level of transport network development in the area. (2 marks)

(iii) Propose measures that can be adopted to improve the transport network of the area. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(d)(i) Topological diagram (6 marks).** A topological diagram (graph) shows only the **nodes** (settlements) and the **links** (roads and tracks between them); distances, directions and curves are ignored. Method: (1) mark the 11 nodes as small circles and name them; (2) read the sheet and draw one straight line for each road or track that joins two nodes directly (no link between two nodes that are only connected through a third one); (3) keep the relative positions roughly as on the map; (4) add a title.

A model reading of the sheet (it must be checked against the original map):

- along the main road from the south-west: Quartier 8 - Manjo Etam - Manengole II - Manengole I - Manengole 3 - Nkong Niny 1 (5 links);
- from Nkong Niny 1 the road to Ebone 1 (1 link), and from Ebone 1 the track to Ebone 2 (1 link);
- from Nkong Niny 1 the road to Nkong Niny 2 (1 link), then Nkong Niny 2 - Ekang Loe (1 link);
- the track from Ebone 2 down to Ekang Loe (1 link) and the road from Ekang Loe to Ekomto (1 link).

![fig-3](gce-al-geography-2022-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Marks: 11 nodes correctly named (3); links correctly drawn (2); graph readable and connected (1).*

**(d)(ii) Beta index (2 marks).** The beta index measures connectivity: $\beta = e / v$, where $e$ is the number of edges (links) and $v$ the number of vertices (nodes).

With $e = 11$ and $v = 11$: $\beta = 11 / 11 = 1.0$.

Interpretation: a value below 1 means a tree with no circuit (a poorly connected network); $\beta = 1$ means a single circuit, the lowest level of a fully connected network; the more circuits, the higher the value (for a planar network of 11 nodes the maximum is $27/11 \approx 2.5$). A value of 1.0 shows that the network is **simple and poorly to moderately developed**: there are few alternative routes, and the cutting of one link (a flood, a landslide) isolates part of the area. (If the candidate counts 12 links the index is $12/11 \approx 1.09$ and the conclusion is the same.)

**(d)(iii) Measures to improve the network (3 marks).**

- Build new links between nodes that are not directly joined, so as to create more circuits (for example a direct road between Nkong Niny 2, Ebone 2 and Manengole 3, and a link from the valley villages to the north).
- Upgrade and tar the earth roads and tracks to all-weather standard, build bridges and culverts, and maintain them regularly (road maintenance funds, community maintenance).
- Provide feeder roads to the isolated settlements, improve public transport, and plan roads outside the Forest Reserve or with minimum damage to it.

*Any three well-explained measures (1 mark each).*
